name: Sodium oxybate (GHB)

lead: Sodium oxybate is the prescription form of GHB, approved in the US for cataplexy and excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy. In recovery discussions it comes up because it deepens slow-wave sleep, which people tie to clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.
It acts at GABA-B receptors and GHB-specific receptors, depressing the central nervous system and increasing slow-wave sleep. No trial has tested it for appearance outcomes.

paras: As a medicine it is dispensed under restricted distribution programs and taken at night under medical supervision for narcolepsy. It is a controlled substance, and the same compound is a controlled drug outside medical use.

The label boxed warning covers central nervous system and respiratory depression and abuse or misuse. Reference sources report overdose risk, especially with alcohol or sedatives. It is Schedule III when marketed for narcolepsy, with restricted distribution.

angle.text: Sodium oxybate is a prescription narcolepsy drug that deepens slow-wave sleep. The idea is deeper sleep, better overnight recovery, then clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is approved for narcolepsy.

lead: Sodium oxybate is the sodium salt of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a central nervous system depressant. As a prescription product it is approved in the US for cataplexy and excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy [1][2]. The same compound is also a controlled drug outside medical use.

It is listed in recovery and sleep discussions because of its reported effect on slow-wave sleep [1]. No published trial has examined it for looksmaxxing outcomes, and the wiki found no community threads that could be cited.

The US label carries a boxed warning for central nervous system depression and for abuse and misuse [2]. Grokipedia reports it is a Schedule III drug when marketed for narcolepsy, with restricted distribution programs [1].
infobox: Rx-only with restricted distribution; US Schedule III as a medicine [1]

paras: Grokipedia reports FDA approval for cataplexy in narcolepsy on 17 July 2002 and for excessive daytime sleepiness in 2005 [1]. Current labeling for Lumryz covers cataplexy or excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy from age 7 [2]. A lower-sodium formulation is approved for idiopathic hypersomnia [1]. Clinical guidelines on narcolepsy and central hypersomnolence include sodium oxybate [3][4][5].

Grokipedia reports the compound acts at GABA-B receptors and at specific GHB receptors, and that endogenous GHB is made from GABA as a neuromodulator [1]. It increases slow-wave sleep in narcolepsy treatment [1].

The label's boxed warning covers CNS depression, including clinically significant respiratory depression and obtundation at recommended amounts, and abuse and misuse [2]. It also lists sleep-disordered breathing, depression and suicidality, and behavioral or psychiatric reactions [2]. Grokipedia reports overdose risks, including coma, particularly when combined with alcohol or sedatives, and that illicit GHB has been misused, including in drug-facilitated crimes [1].

A multicenter randomized placebo-controlled trial and a later study evaluated sodium oxybate in narcolepsy, reporting improvements in cataplexy and daytime sleepiness [6][7]. Reviews also examine it in alcohol use disorder [8]. Pharmacology work has examined sleep spindles and memory with GHB [9]. Research on sleep and cerebrospinal fluid amyloid-beta and tau is not specific to sodium oxybate [10]. No studies were found testing sodium oxybate for appearance.

timeline.event: FDA approves sodium oxybate for cataplexy in narcolepsy [1].
Once-nightly extended-release sodium oxybate and a low-sodium formulation approved, per reference sources [1].
